World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Alice Springs riot another flashpoint for town trying to heal from heartbreak
World.content:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of her family.

In between the projectiles being hurled by rioters and tear gas being thrown by police, another shocking reality of last Thursday's Alice Springs riot presented itself on the night.

Young children, under 10-years-old, were among those rushing to the front of the crowd and throwing rocks towards emergency service workers at Alice Springs Hospital.

While they were the minority in the crowd, seeing such young children involved in a violent affray will likely be alarming to many; not least in the Central Australian community.

Loading...

The riot exploded outside the hospital following the arrest of Kumanjayi Little Baby's alleged murderer, 47-year-old Jefferson Lewis.

The incident was undoubtedly a demonstration of collective grief and anger after the five-year-old's tragic death was announced earlier that same day, but elders and authorities believe there was more at play than just those emotions.

In targeting police officers, senior Alyawarre man Michael Liddle said the riot was also a spillover of rage from "people who are very angry with the systems" in the Northern Territory.

"The same systems that create safety and less harm, keeping people safe in Alice Springs," he said.

"Through that incident we had police cars being damaged and ambulances being damaged.

"And when you take those services out, well, we've got a scenario of no rules, no laws, and people become hurt."

Michael Liddle criticised the violent behaviour directed towards emergency service staff at the riots last week. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

As well as the unrest out the front of the hospital, rioters also ransacked and looted a service station on the other side of the road.

As of Wednesday, 30 people had been arrested over this and another supermarket looting, and charged with aggravated burglary, theft, damage to property and other charges.

NT Police Commissioner Martin Dole said on Sunday that CCTV footage released of those incidents did not show "people processing grief in relation to the death of Baby Kumanjayi".

"What you will see is criminal behaviour, plain and simple," he said.

Loading...

The riot came at the end of a week which saw the Alice Springs community come together in the expansive search for Kumanjayi Little Baby, before the devastating discovery of her body in bushland.

Even during the riot, there were brief moments of togetherness, one of which was captured on camera when a crowd member tightly hugged a police officer clutching a riot shield.

A protester at the riot outside of Alice Springs hospital could be seen hugging a police officer on the front lines. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Another Alice flashpoint turns political

Thursday's riot was hardly the first flashpoint seen in Alice Springs in recent past.

Over the years, there have been short-term and long-term solutions posed, including after last week’s riot, the immediate restriction of takeaway alcohol sales.

The town has had youth curfews imposed, Aboriginal town camp alcohol bans lifted then reimposed, and ongoing national attention over youth crime.

At night Alice Springs looks like 'Grand Theft Auto' Kids hooning around in stolen cars. Driving head-on at police. Filming the action. A youth crime wave has engulfed Alice Springs — and the community is desperate for solutions.

There was also the territory's longest-ever running coronial inquest held in the town, following the police shooting death of Kumanjayi Walker in Yuendumu in 2019.

In early 2023, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese flew into the town to announce $250 million would be spent on trying to improve outcomes for people in Central Australia.

There are a lot of complex overlapping issues contributing to the situation in the region's remote and town Aboriginal communities.

Among those, there's pronounced social factors like overcrowded housing, low school attendance figures and ever-increasing rates of Indigenous incarceration.

There's also many visible examples of extreme intergenerational disadvantage, which some Central Australian Aboriginal elders have repeatedly said is driven in part by decades of failed government policy and inequality.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan said now is the time for the Commonwealth to "get its hands dirty" in trying to find some practical outcomes for the region, not just throwing money at it.

Malarndirri McCarthy conceded the government still had a lot of work to do to meet Closing the Gap targets. (ABC: Matt Roberts)

Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy was asked by 7.30 host Sarah Ferguson this week if the millions spent by her government was translating into real results.

"When we look at Closing the Gap and the targets that we have, we know we've got a hell of a lot of work to continue to do, but we must do it with the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community," Ms McCarthy said in response.

" Not for them, not against them, but always with them. "

So what will happen next?

Over the coming weeks, a difficult tug-of-war between perspectives looks sure to play out.

Will the Commonwealth continue to resist calls from the Coalition to trigger an inquiry or royal commission?

Or will it flip on the issue as it did over calls for a royal commission on the Bondi massacre?

For now, there have been calls from the family for a pause on politicising the issue.

Whatever comes next, for now the family of Kumanjayi Little Baby is conducting sorry business and grieving for its precious little life lost.

World.title: Nikita Tzsyu maintains incredible family record as world title bid looms
World.content:
Emerging Australian boxing superstar Nikita Tszyu has lived up to his word and taken out big-talking and tough Spaniard Oscar Diaz to edge closer to a world-title shot.

Tszyu improved his unbeaten record to 13-0 with an emphatic sixth-round stoppage in the pair's super-welterweight showdown in Newcastle on Wednesday night.

Forging his own path after living in the shadows of his Hall-of-Fame father, Kostya, and fellow world title-winning brother Tim, Tszyu is now potentially one win away from securing his own shot at global glory.

The likes of superstar Keith Thurman and fellow American Tony Harrison, who Tim KO'ed in 2023 to win the WBO super-welterweight belt, are being touted as Tszyu's possible next targets.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Tszyu entered his latest contest ranked sixth with the IBF and is now tipped to climb to as high as number three in the division's pecking order after savagely ending Diaz's unbeaten record.

The so-called "Butcher" lived up to all expectations with a comprehensive display at the "Tszyu-Castle" Entertainment Centre.

Looking physically imposing in career-best shape, the home favourite dominated from the first bell.

He landed several blows in the opening round, then dropped the Spaniard in the second with a big left.

Tszyu continued the onslaught in round three despite the flurry of punches to Diaz's head, only provoking a wry smile from Diaz, nicknamed "The Bull' or 'El Toro" after winning all of his previous 16 fights.

But his chin could cop only so much.

After withstanding another fierce combination in round five, Diaz finally succumbed after Tszyu floored the European with a devastating left-right barrage in the sixth stanza.

Diaz's camp initially protested after seeing their man cop more blows while on his knees on the ropes, and Tszyu apologised.

Then they mercifully informed the referee that Diaz could not continue.

With Kostya (18-0) and Tim (23-0) on home soil, Tszyu's win extends the record of Australian boxing's most famous family to an incredible 54-0.

Anthony Mundine watched as his son Rahim defeated Lance McDonald. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

On Wednesday night's undercard, another son of a gun also maintained his undefeated professional record as Rahim Mundine scored a unanimous points win over Lance McDonald in a five-round super-welterweight stoush.

The victory was Mundine's third since debuting under crushing expectations four years ago.

But the 24-year-old son of ex-triple world champion Anthony Mundine could not escape the shadow of his polarising father.

"My dad's the most hated athlete ever in this country," he said after being booed and jeered by the Newcastle crowd after the three judges awarded him the bout 49-46, 49-46 and 48-47.

"I won easy, but he's a real tough competitor. I landed cleaner shots."

AAP

World.title: NSW gun industry calls for buyback to be scrapped amid plummeting sales
World.content:
States and territories are facing renewed pressure to buy back guns in the wake of the Bondi massacre, but the industry warns fewer guns are already being sold.

An updated national gun control framework and gun buyback scheme were among the recommendations in the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion's interim report by commissioner Virginia Bell.

The state and federal governments passed sweeping new regulations last year that put limits on the number of guns an individual can own and reclassified certain firearms.

However, NSW is the only state to sign on to the National Gun Buyback Scheme, with several states going ahead with their own schemes.

Nicky Bourke, who owns a gun shop in the western NSW town of Dubbo, said the recent changes had led to a 90 per cent drop in business and customers failing to collect their firearms.

Gun shop owner Nicky Bourke holds an Australian-made Taipan X pump-action rifle, which will be re-categorised under the new laws. (Supplied: Nicky Bourke)

Under the new laws, licensed individuals in NSW are limited to four firearms, while primary producers are able to own up to 10.

"Not only are we sitting on stock left over from Christmas, we have numerous lay-bys and deposits on firearms that have not been picked up," Ms Bourke said.

" [Buyers] have either met the capacity or they just don't want to come and collect their lay-bys because of the gun reform. "

Ms Bourke has laid off casuals to focus on retaining permanent staff.

"It's quite disheartening when we used to be a really thriving, busy retail store," she said.

Long delays in licence approvals

Sydney gun shop director Gary Georgiou said the reforms had led to a spike in licence applications and a delay in approvals.

"We've had licence applications that have gone in just before Christmas, just after the Bondi terror attack, and they've yet to receive their licences," he said.

"They will then need to put in permits to acquire … so we could be well into September [or] October before a new shooter can buy a gun."

A linear bolt action rifle (top) will require additional approval under new firearms laws, alongside a conventional bolt action rifle, which will not. (Supplied: Michael Corkhill)

Mr Georgiou said sales were down by about 70 per cent at his store.

" People are unsure, so they're just not buying and not wanting to buy for the reason that they might not get their money back. "

Industry questions buyback

Mr Georgiou said the buyback was a "waste of money" and has called for it to be scrapped.

"All people are going to do is hand in their rubbish guns or guns that don't work or the guns that they don't care about and then potentially buy new ones," he said.

Mr Georgiou said while that would be good for gun shops, it would not make Australia safer.

Shooting Industry Foundation of Australia chief executive James Walsh agrees and points to the lack of state and territory support for the federal buyback.

"If this is meant to be the centrepiece of the government's policy, then it's a failure," he said.

James Walsh is calling for more government support for the gun industry in NSW after tougher legislation was passed. (Supplied: James Walsh)

He said sales data gathered by the foundation in NSW showed a drop of 60-80 per cent across the state.

"We've been pushing the NSW government for industry support and payments as a result of their rushed legislation," he said.

"But to date, they've been silent on that."

The 'intent' of firearms policy

University of Sydney professor of public health Joel Negin said the federal government may have to foot the bill for the buyback scheme if it could not get an agreement with all the states.

"If the finance is an issue then the federal government … should put the funds together for the National Firearms Register … or the gun buyback if that's what needs to happen in order to enhance public safety," he said.

Joel Negin has rejected calls to scrap the gun buyback. (ABC News: Quentin Theron)

Professor Negin rejected the gun industry's calls for the buyback to be scrapped, saying public safety must be prioritised.

"The viability of a commercial enterprise to sell firearms is not the overriding intent of firearms policy," he said.

Professor Negin said a multi-pronged response to the Bondi attack was needed.

"Firearms mortality, homicides and, really importantly, suicides came down in the period after Port Arthur," he said.

"Not just because of the buyback, but because of the suite of changes."

New laws in NSW limit the number of firearms an individual can own. (ABC News: Sam Clark)

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has indicated he would support all 14 recommendations in the interim report from the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion.

The recommendations included a call for commonwealth, state and territory governments to prioritise a consistent national firearms agreement, together with a national gun buyback scheme.

In a statement, NSW Minister for Police and Counter-terrorism Yasmin Catley said the government planned to "significantly uplift" the NSW Firearms Registry to ensure it could continue processing firearm licences.

Ms Catley said the NSW government was also working closely with the federal government on the details of the buyback scheme.

NSW Liberal leader Kellie Sloane told the ABC she supported tough gun laws, but they must be fair and workable for farmers and sporting shooters.

"That doesn't mean we need to reduce the cap, it doesn't mean we need to weaken the laws," she said.

World.title: Exit 8 explores the mundane horror of life in a loop
World.content:
The feeling that the everyday world no longer makes sense is one that author and filmmaker Genki Nakamura is keenly aware of when he rides the subway in Tokyo.

The labyrinthine passages of the Tokyo Metro are packed with commuters barely acknowledging each other's existence.

It's in these spaces between locations that psychological horror film Exit 8 is set.

Nakamura, who is in Australia for the Melbourne Writers Festival, says the film explores the feeling of disconnection from reality.

Kazunari Ninomiya plays the Lost Man struggling to escape the supernatural hallways in Exit 8. (Supplied: Umbrella Entertainment)

"Most people are going around their homes and workplaces, they're doing a loop in their daily lives," he says.

"In that loop they see violence and war in reality and in their smartphones, but they pretend not to see it.

"There are a lot of people there, but they're all looking at their smartphones, only thinking about themselves.

"It's a very unique space in Tokyo. I wanted to make the theme of the film the root of all the guilt of all urban dwellers."

In the film Kazunari Ninomiya plays a character known only as the Lost Man, who becomes trapped in an ever-looping metro station corridor, brightly lit and clean.

Everything seems ordinary until he's instructed by a metro station sign to find Exit 8, to watch for anomalies and to turn back if he sees something weird or to push on if the path looks normal.

Incorrectly placed door handles, different lighting, or peering eyes on s that track the Lost Man are unsettling signs of the aberrations contained within.

The signs are designed to look exactly as they appear in the Tokyo Metro, but with strange instructions such as "Do not overlook anomalies". (Supplied: Umbrella Entertainment)

It's an adaption of the popular photorealistic video game of the same name by Kotake Create, where players must investigate a hallway on their way to the end of the station.

The game itself became popular online with video game live-streamers and their audiences, a factor that was quickly noticed by Nakamura, who played the game himself and watched the stories emerge within other people's play-throughs.

"Shigeru Miyamoto, the creator of Super Mario, said that a good game is fun to play and at the same time — it's fun to watch someone else play," Nakamura says.

Before: The hallway as it appears in the video game Exit 8. . . After: The hallway recreated in the film adaption. . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE The hallway as it appears in the video game Exit 8. / The hallway recreated in the film adaption.

"What was interesting was that it was a game with very simple rules and loops, but there were different stories for each of the players.

"When I decided to make the game a film, I wanted to make the movie a new state of that world."

The hallways of Hitchcock and Kubrick

Nakamura said the film was shot over a month, with two identical versions of the hallway built in order to use a single physical shot to create the loop without visual effects.

The cast would walk along the length of one section of the hallway, then ride a bike to the other end of the opposite hallway, catch their breath and start walking through again.

Nakamura says even the crew began to lose track of where they were in those hallways.

"We spent a month every day in that pure white space, we were going to go crazy and even we didn't know where we were," Nakamura says.

"So we called the first one Hitchcock and the second one Kubrick to keep track."

The video game Exit 8 uses photorealistic graphics, which have been matched perfectly by the set designers in the film. (Supplied: Kotake Create)

Adapting a game to film

Nakamura told ABC Arts it was a worrying task to adapt the world of the interactive video game for the silver screen.

"I was very scared, it was a very terrible prospect, because nobody knows how to make that kind of film, so it's very dangerous," he says.

"When I first handed the script to the staff, they told me that there are only 16 scenes in this movie.

"The staff all looked anxious and asked me how to make this into a movie."

"I told them that they didn't have to worry, because I didn't know what kind of movie it would be. I wanted to see something that I didn't know how to make."

The film was selected for Cannes Film Festival and made its premiere in May 2025.

It was the first time a video game adaptation was selected for the festival and Nakamura said seeing all types of audiences enjoying the movie was a relief.

"When the film premiered at Cannes Film Festival … what made me happy was that there were a lot of cinephiles, a lot of filmmakers, but at the same time there were a lot of students and game fans in the same movie theatre," he says.

He hopes that eventually, like the main character, audiences will begin to look up and acknowledge the other people around them when moving through the world.

"I'm hoping that watching this movie at least gives people a little bit of pause to think not getting swept away in this deluge of apathetic doom scrolling and have another think about how they spend their days.

"It would be very good to see that."

Genki Nakamura will appear at Melbourne Writers Festival May 7-10. Exit 8 is now showing in cinemas.

World.title: 'Plenty of fish' but algae bloom 'uncertainty' persists at SA tourist town
World.content:
In the Yorke Peninsula town of Port Hughes, casting a line off the jetty is a beloved pastime.

But beneath the surface, the damage caused by South Australia's harmful algal bloom is continuing to be documented, even as government water testing shows reduced levels of karenia across most of the coastline.

"The colour that used to be there is no longer present at the site," marine biologist and creative director of the Great Southern Reef Foundation Stefan Andrews said.

"The amount of fish life, even though there's still plenty of fish down there, the fish diversity has decreased significantly.

" Overall, it's just looking quite tired and sad … a shell of what this place used to look like. "

Port Hughes jetty is a popular fishing spot. (ABC News: Jack Stephens)

Mr Andrews has been routinely diving and capturing underwater vision off the coast of Port Hughes and documenting environmental changes since elevated levels of the bloom were first detected in late March this year.

"What's been interesting is looking at even small levels of those harmful algal species being present, how much damage actually still has been able to occur," he said

"When you start looking at the pylons, that's where the real visible difference is from the before and after, and that's continued to deteriorate.

"There's definitely things that are missing, and there's definitely things that are looking sick and slow and sluggish, and there's some things that seem to be holding on OK for now."

The first elevated levels of karenia were detected at the Port Hughes jetty on March 30, 2026. (Supplied: Stefan Andrews, Great Southern Reef Foundation)

According to the Department of Primary Industries and Regions, the first elevated levels of karenia were detected at the Port Hughes jetty on March 30, 2026.

Algae levels peaked a week later on April 6, when 16,850 karenia cells per litre were detected.

The SA government classifies any reading above 10,000 cells per litre as being elevated.

Latest water sampling conducted on April 29 shows levels at Port Hughes have dropped and are sitting at the low reading of 1,936 cells per litre.

Algae levels peaked on April 6, when 16,850 karenia cells per litre were detected. (Supplied: Stefan Andrews, Great Southern Reef Foundation)

"While the symptoms of the bloom may have been gone from certain areas, the ongoing impacts to the ecosystem are very much long-term," Mr Andrews said.

"To say that the bloom is over is a naive way of putting it because there's the impacts continue to unfold and be ongoing and we don't know that it's over.

"We don't know when it's going to come back and hit other areas even more, so there's still so much uncertainty about what's ahead."

Marine biologist Stefan Andrews says the impact of the algae bloom on the ecosystem is long-term. (ABC News: Jack Stephens)

'Dramatic drop' in business

Port Hughes Fishing Charters owner Thomas Hams said his business has seen a "dramatic drop" in business in recent months compared to last year.

"A lot more people are scared as such to get out on the water, plus with all the restrictions they've put in place," Mr Hams said.

Thomas Hams says the bloom is affecting his fishing charter business. (Supplied: Thomas Hams)

As of May 1, a ban on southern calamari for commercial, recreational and charter boats fishing in both the Spencer Gulf and Gulf St Vincent came into place due to depleted fish stocks.

A spawning closure is also in place for King George Whiting across both Gulfs until July 31.

Mr Hams said while some species, such as snapper, are in abundance, he has noticed a reduction in calamari.

On his recreational charters, he said customers are always curious about the impacts of the bloom.

"It's definitely something that's spooking people, and they ring up and ask how it's going," he said.

" We're lucky enough we haven't really been affected that badly … which gives people a bit of peace of mind when they get out there and it's crystal-clear blue waters. "

Mr Hams said he suspects the price of fuel, despite the recent price drop, has also had an impact on potential customers.

"For the last month, it's been pretty hard, bearing all the extra costs with all that and trying to keep our price the same as what it always is."

Levels of karenia have reduced at Port Hughes. (Supplied: Stefan Andrews, Great Southern Reef Foundation)

Port Hughes General Store and tackle shop owner Luke Pridham said even before the bloom was detected at Port Hughes, the misconception that the bloom had spread to the whole of the peninsula was damaging to tourism.

"The Yorke Peninsula is a big place and we had no sign of it here, and people would ring up, cancel their bookings or say they're not coming up due to the fact the algae bloom's here," he said.

"That was probably the most disappointing thing, the misreporting on it."

Port Hughes General Store owner Luke Pridham. (ABC News: Jack Stephens)

Mr Pridham said, despite the uncertainty with the bloom and fuel prices, his business has recorded one of the busiest Easter holiday periods they have seen in three years.

"I would say the fuel had more of an impact than the algae bloom did," Mr Pridham said.

"We have escaped it pretty well; it was the worry of what it was going to create … got to people more than what actually has [happened].

"It's obviously probably done damage out there that we don't see, but to this point we haven't had a massive impact on us, really.

"I'd be a little bit hesitant to say it's [the bloom] all of a sudden disappeared."

World.title: Paddock-to-plate revival as farmers grapple with surging food freight costs
World.content:
Global attention on the vulnerability of food supply chains has inspired a paddock-to-plate revival, but not all farmers and shoppers can benefit.

As the Iran War escalated, retailer Angela Nason said growers and consumers flooded her Far North Queensland produce store with inquiries.

"I have put on two more day crew to handle that amount of people coming in, [and] we've opened up on a Saturday now too," she said.

As the cost of each kilometre food travels explodes, supermarkets are also facing pressure to absorb the price rises associated with the disruption.

But the model only works if the paddocks are close to the plates, taking shortening the supply chain off the table for many.

Trucking loop-de-loop

Ms Nason's store is on the Atherton Tablelands at Mareeba, west of Cairns.

Angela Nason sources produce for her store from local Atherton Tablelands growers. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

The region is a horticultural powerhouse, producing citrus, avocados, bananas, mangoes and other crops valued at almost $748 million.

But before any of that produce is available in a local supermarket, it first has to travel thousands of kilometres to wholesale markets in Brisbane, Sydney or Melbourne, only to be trucked back to retailers in the north.

Ms Nason said farmers struggling with rising freight costs were looking for ways to sell closer to home.

"My phone rings continuously off the hook, we have loads of farmers ringing us for help, pretty much on a daily basis," Ms Nason said.

Ms Nason has opened a second store in Cairns. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

At Jonsson's Farmers Market in Cairns, operations manager Joe Cincota has also noticed more foot traffic.

"We've undergone a bit of a transformation in the store and re-looked at our pricing, trying to do a better job with pricing and give customers a better deal," he said.

But he said there were limits to how much could be supplied locally, relying on central markets to fill in the gaps.

"We can't get everything local ... but we are the luckiest state in terms of we grow a great proportion of especially the fruits that we use," he said.

"The freshness comes from literally buying direct from the grower where we can."

Jonsson Farmers Markets sources as much produce as possible from local growing regions. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

Growers on board

About 1,300 kilometres away at Rosedale, north of Bundaberg, Luke Tresize and De'Arne Chapman hope to expand their regenerative farming business, Golden Hill Farm.

They farm cattle, sheep, poultry and pigs.

Ms Chapman said she had noticed increased demand for paddock-to-plate options as more consumers explored what was in their food.

"I think because of social media, people want to know where their food is coming from," she said.

" They want that traceability, they want lower kilometres being travelled to get their food. "

Luke Tresize and De'Arne Chapman are regenerative farmers based in Rosedale. (ABC Rural: Tayla Larsen)

The couple's meat is processed at Biggenden before it is packaged and then sold at local markets.

They have purchased an on-farm butcher room in a bid to streamline their business and cut costs.

They said it should be operational by September.

"The plan is to be able to utilise other farms in the region who are farming similar to us, which will give the local community access to more local beef, pork and lamb," Mr Tresize said.

"We're living in an amazing food-growing region here, so why are we chasing food from Tasmania or Victoria when it can all be grown here?"

Mr Tresize and Ms Chapman have purchased an on-farm butcher room. (ABC Rural: Tayla Larsen)

Local markets not for all

Ebony Faichney is a horticultural farming consultant with Farmour, based in Mareeba.

She said farmers could gain benefits by diversifying their markets, but it was harder for bigger growers to sell their produce locally.

"A lot of our really small farms, their local supply chain works perfectly and they can sell the majority of their crop to local fruit shops," she said.

"But when you start to scale up, [like] some of our larger players here on the Tablelands and Mareeba Dimbulah area, unfortunately, the sheer volume of fruit that they're producing just can't be absorbed by our local market."

Queensland Fruit and Vegetable Growers chief executive Scott Kompo-Harms said the paddock-to-plate model was not always an option for those shopping at farmers' markets in more urban areas, like Brisbane, where produce tended to come from central markets, meaning there was still a transport element.

However, he said local markets provided a great opportunity to educate consumers, especially in a time of global uncertainty.

"I still think that is a fundamental challenge for our industry in ensuring that the vast majority of their consumers actually understand what it takes to get [produce] on the shelf," Mr Kompo-Harms said.

"[Local markets] can just create that little bit stronger connection."

World.title: Live: Israel strikes Beirut for first time since Hezbollah ceasefire
World.content:
While some news outlets are reporting Iran and the United States are the closest they've been to a deal, it's important to put things in context.

US officials and the president have expressed optimism about a deal being imminent multiple times before and we still don't have one.

There has been mixed messaging from US officials about the war in the Middle East.

The White House is also reportedly concerned about divisions within the Iranian leadership so it may be difficult for them to get consensus across factions.

And there's a lot of mixed messaging coming out of the White House.

Yesterday Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Operation Epic Fury — which this war has been dubbed — was 'over'.

This morning, Donald Trump said 'Epic Fury will be at an end' if Iran agrees to the United States' terms.

He also declared again that the US had already won the war.

It just shows how conflicted the messaging is, how fast moving negotiations are and that a final deal is by no means guaranteed.

World.title: 'I'll show no mercy': Charity founder faces 'tickle torture' allegations
World.content:
A teenager who was hogtied and beaten by a decorated youth advocate says he feels let down by the justice system after his abuser avoided jail time over the "disgusting" assault.

Fletcher Wicks* was one of five teenagers, aged 14 to 17, who Cody Schaeffer pleaded guilty to assaulting at his south-east Queensland home between 2021 and 2023.

The ABC has spoken with other men since the March sentencing who claim the former Order of Australia recipient also asked to tie them up and tickle them for payment, with allegations dating back to more than a decade ago.

Fletcher Wicks was one of five teenagers who Schaeffer pleaded guilty to assaulting between 2021 and 2023. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Fletcher was 15, and Schaeffer was in his late 20s, when they met at a camp advocating for youth mental health.

The week-long camps were organised by Borderline Australia, a charity founded by Schaeffer. They featured Australian influencers and celebrities, as well as activities such as kayaking and archery, a formal night, and team-building exercises.

Schaeffer was well-connected and "easy to talk to", presenting himself as someone you could trust and be yourself around, Fletcher says.

He quickly became Fletcher's "best friend and mentor" and was close with his entire family, often joining them for dinners at his childhood home.

"[A group of us teenagers] we were over Cody's house every weekend," he said. "He'd come pick us up, and we'd all chill at his house, watch documentaries and movies and eat lots of KFC."

Fletcher was 15 years old when he met Schaeffer, who was then in his late 20s. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

One day, Schaeffer asked Fletcher, then 16, if he could tie him up and whip his feet with a coat hanger for $100.

In an interview with the ABC, Fletcher said Schaeffer told him to keep it a secret.

"As a young, eager kid, $100 was a lot at the time," Fletcher said.

"He was like 'just with the bros, it's a bro kind of thing' … I thought if it's just with the bros, how bad could it be?"

But when he cried out for Schaeffer to stop, he continued.

"I moved the gag out of my mouth because it wasn't too tight, and I started yelling 'stop, stop, stop' and he was like 'you're almost there', and he kept going," Fletcher says.

" It got to the point where I was crying. I just couldn't bear the pain. "

Schaeffer admitted to paying five children to hogtie them and whip their feet with coat hangers during his sentencing at the Brisbane Magistrates Court.

The court heard that Schaeffer ignored the boys when they told him to stop and placed duct tape over some victims' eyes and mouths, which they did not consent to.

Magistrate Zachary Sarra described the offending as "insidious" and "disturbing".

Schaeffer's offending was described as "insidious" and "disturbing." (Supplied: Instagram)

During defence submissions, Magistrate Sarra said Schaeffer's actions of binding and gagging children could have caused problems with their breathing or sent them into shock.

"That is very dangerous," he said.

Schaeffer was sentenced to nine months' jail, wholly suspended for 18 months, over six charges of common assault.

After sentencing, the Governor-General accepted Schaeffer's resignation as a member of the Order of Australia, an honour awarded to him for his youth advocacy work.

Fletcher says that after the assault, Schaeffer downplayed what occurred.

"At the time, I felt pretty embarrassed and pretty sick in my own skin … there was no remorse," he told the ABC.

"He just acted like everything was normal. He just blew it off and didn't show much empathy."

The week-long camps often featured Australian influencers and celebrities. (Supplied)

Fletcher says Schaeffer continued messaging him after the assault, offering more money to do it again.

Fletcher believes a heftier penalty should have been handed down.

"'I feel like I've been punched in the face or pushed into the shadows," Fletcher says. "It's brought back that trauma of it."

Fletcher told the ABC Schaeffer asked him if he could tie him up and whip his feet with a coat hanger for $100. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

'I'll show no mercy'

Jason Kurt* also met Schaeffer through the Borderline camps. But he says that after the event was over, Schaeffer kept messaging him.

"He would Snapchat me all the time, and he was 29 or 30," Jason said.

When he was 16, Jason alleges Schaeffer asked if he would like to be tied up and tickled on camera, claiming it's a "good laugh and great money."

"It's for an Asian dating site (not accessible in Australia) haha so you're fine! Super confidential," Schaeffer wrote in messages seen by the ABC.

"But it's like $300–500 per 15 min shoot!

Fletcher was 15 when he met Schaeffer at a week-long camp organised by Schaeffer's charity, Borderline Australia. (Supplied)

"No-one will know you do it, identity is covered. And no it's not porn."

In the messages, Schaeffer said he was only making the offer because Jason was a friend, but "from an outside perspective it could be seen as inappropriate."

When Jason took a screenshot of the messages, Schaffer accused him of a "betrayal of trust".

"Yeah cool. You go and tell people stuff that is damaging to my reputation — even though it was a passing offer between us, a chill thing that's also a laugh and something I thought would have stayed between us because we're mates," Schaffer wrote.

Jason was not involved in the court case and told the ABC that he reported these messages to the police with his parents, but "nothing happened."

A Queensland police spokesperson said: "Investigations into all formal complaints have concluded — subject to no new information being received."

"In the absence of any new information and no new disclosures, investigations into the matter have been finalised."

Schaeffer ran the Borderline camps. (Supplied)

Other allegations date back to more than a decade ago.

In the 2010s, Jesse Roberts* was offered work with Schaeffer's talent agency, Codez.

On Instagram, Codez was described as a Brisbane-based management company "for Australia's biggest upcoming performers".

Jesse alleges that during his paid employment, he received messages from Schaffer asking him to partake in "tickle torture" or the "duct tape" challenge.

In messages seen by the ABC, Schaeffer offered Jesse $50 to wrap him in duct tape for one hour.

"$70 and you've got a deal," Jesse joked.

"Deal. $70 includes tickle torture," Schaffer wrote.

Former youth advocated sentenced for assaulting teens The court heard Cody Schaeffer, who founded Borderline Australia, paid each boy to be "hogtied" and "have their feet slapped with coat hangers".

When Jesse did not respond, Schaeffer messaged: "or don't reply den [sic.] wow."

The next day, Schaeffer asked Jesse again, "when are you going to do your duct tape challenge".

"Dunno. Just thinking of how to fight my fear of losing dignity," Jesse responded.

Schaeffer replied, "HAHAHAHA DO IT C**T… just yolo.

"Or nolo," Jesse wrote.

At the time, Jesse says he was uncomfortable but thought the exchange was a dark joke.

"It was just a shocking thing to experience," he said. "I'm a father, and now I'm reliving it," he said.

"Bringing Schaeffer to justice will help me heal, as well as the victims."

Schaeffer founded Borderline Australia. (Supplied)

Vince Heard* also worked for Schaeffer's talent agency in the 2010s. Both Jesse and Vince were in their 20s when they met Schaeffer and neither were party to the criminal case against him.

"I was pretty heavily in debt and had a poor paying job … There was definitely a power imbalance," Vince said.

In 2016 messages, seen by the ABC, Schaeffer offered Vince payment to do "the tickle torture challenge."

"He was offering me money, tickets to Broncos games," Vince said. "I've always hated tickling since I was a kid."

One day, at Schaeffer's former Brisbane apartment, Vince says he reluctantly agreed.

He says Schaeffer duct taped his wrists and ankles and started tickling him.

"I remember yelling at him to stop and that I was really uncomfortable with it, and he was laughing the whole way through," Vince said.

The same year, after the alleged incident, Schaeffer messaged Vince, "rip out the duct tape and tickle torture again. I know you don't want that hahahahaha."

"I would actually murder you," Vince wrote.

"Hahahahhaha it's going to happen again. I'll show no mercy," Schaeffer replied.

Schaeffer continued to message Vince years after the alleged incident, when he was working a Brisbane radio job, offering him money.

"I WANT YOU TO. DO IT DOG. Jonathan Thurston Lunch & Meet & Greet Tuesday at Suncorp. RNB Fridays live and so much more. All you have to do is the 5-minute tickle challenge hehehehe."

In another message years on , Schaffer wrote, "Would you rather duct tape and tickle challenge or duct tape and hit with a coat hanger challenge. You decide because one of them is happening," Schaffer said.

Vince replied, "I'd prefer to be hit with a coat hanger. Tickle is the worst honestly."

Schaeffer then responded, "okay well game on xx You get duct taped or zip tied and hit with a coat hanger. It's happening."

Vince says he only went ahead with Schaeffer's suggestions the first time and that he tried to maintain the friendship and a sense of normalcy as he did not want to accept the alleged incident.

Brisbane charity founder Cody Schaeffer (Supplied: Facebook)

Then he saw the ABC's reporting that Schaeffer had been arrested last year.

"I was [in my mid 20s] at the time … And then seeing that he did this to these 14, 15-year-old boys and how powerless I felt at the time, I couldn't imagine how they would've felt," he said.

Magistrate questioned charges and basis for sentencing

At Schaeffer's sentencing in March, Magistrate Sarra quizzed the legal parties on more than one occasion about why more serious charges were not laid.

At the beginning of the proceeding, Magistrate Sarra checked that Schaeffer understood the charges against him, before remarking he was "still trying to work it out" himself.

After a brief explanation by the prosecution, Magistrate Sarra asked "so if they're adults, and they're consenting adults, he probably wouldn't be charged?"

The prosecution somewhat agreed that may have been the case, to which Magistrate Sarra said Schaeffer's conduct sounded "like an unusual perversion".

"It's not the normal thing that you do with people," he said.

Magistrate Sarra made a reference to priests and politicians who had "interfered with children", as being categorised as paedophiles and asked, "is that not suggested in this case?".

Brisbane charity founder Cody Schaeffer (Supplied: Facebook)

To this, prosecutor Kacie Atkinson responded she had to "be careful not to suggest that there was any sexual gratification" on Schaeffer's part.

Later in the hearing, Magistrate Sarra said the offending sounded like a form of "torture" despite the children consenting "to an extent".

Ms Atkinson told the court although it hurt them at the time, Schaeffer's victims did not receive "any actual physical injuries", which was the reason for the common assault charges.

Magistrate Sarra replied that it "sounds whack to me".

Ms Atkinson later said the only basis for the assaults "would either be based on sexual gratification or in some form of cruel and unusual punishment".

"We are not alleging here, as we cannot, that there was a sexual basis to the offending, which does leave the inference this was a punishment of some form," she said.

When Magistrate Sarra asked if the children were in fact being punished, Ms Atkinson said she did not have any information about Schaeffer's motivation.

Magistrate Sarra acknowledged the prosecutor was trying her best to categorise the "clearly bizarre" offending, but queried whether it was sadistic in nature, which she said it was not.

When lawyer Danielle Egan submitted that Schaeffer's victims had "initially willingly engaged", Magistrate Sarra interjected that this was only because he was their mentor.

"He is their role model, he's the person who these children invested their trust, and he took advantage of their trust," he said.

" I don't know anyone who would say I am happy to be bound and gagged and I'm even happy for you to put duct tape across my face so I can't even see. "

Magistrate Sarra said it was even worse that Schaeffer was paying the children "to be beaten".

Ms Egan accepted the offending was serious but said the "basis of the plea" and the "criminality of the offending" only extended to the fact that after the victims said stop, "it continued on".

To that, Magistrate Sarra said "when you start binding people, it starts sounding like deprivation of liberty", which is another criminal offence.

Ms Egan said "there were reasons" he was charged with common assault only, to which Ms Atkinson agreed, but no further explanation was provided to the court.

Ultimately, Magistrate Sarra could only sentence Schaeffer on the charges before him, and based on submissions made by his lawyer and the prosecution to the court.

Fletcher said he feels let down by the justice system after Schaeffer escaped jail time over the assaults. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

By talking publicly about the assault, Fletcher hopes he can erase the stigma.

"It's definitely that stigma of you're a man … you don't really want to open up because it makes you seem weak," he said.

" I want other people to know what Cody Schaeffer's done and how he's impacted our lives and how he's made us victims of this really disgusting crime. "

The ABC has contacted Schaeffer for comment.

World.title: ‘Mouth of the South’: Billionaire CNN founder Ted Turner dies
World.content:
Updated BusinessCompaniesVale ‘Mouth of the South’: Billionaire CNN founder Ted Turner dies David Bauder Updated May 7, 2026 — 6:45am ,first published 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ted Turner, the outspoken television pioneer who created a media empire and transformed the news business by creating CNN and introducing the 24-hour cable news cycle, has died aged 87. The father of five died on Wednesday surrounded by his family, according to Turner Enterprises, the company that oversees his vast business interests and investments. Jane Fonda and Ted Turner, who were married from 1991 to 2001, pose together at an event in 2013. AP Turner’s empire expanded far beyond media – owning professional sports teams in Atlanta and huge chunks of the American West. He raced yachts too, defending the America’s Cup in 1977. He donated a stunning $US1 billion ($1.4 billion) to United Nations charities and fuelled conservation efforts.



Turner married three women – most famously actor Jane Fonda – and earned the nicknames “Captain Outrageous” and “The Mouth of the South.” Related Article Updated

Media & marketing James Murdoch makes $418m offer for US media assets: report He once bragged: “If only I had a little humility, I’d be perfect.” He was slowed in later years by Lewy body dementia. Long since out of the television business, he concentrated on philanthropy. His garrulous personality sometimes overshadowed a driven, risk-taking business acumen. By the time he sold his Turner Broadcasting System to Time Warner Inc. in a 1996 media megadeal, Turner had turned his late father’s billboard company into a global conglomerate that included seven major cable networks, three professional sports teams and a pair of hit movie studios.



US President Donald Trump, reacting to Turner’s death, called him “one of the Greats of All Time.” “Whenever I needed him, he was there, always willing to fight for a good cause!” Trump posted on social media. Turner’s signature achievement was creating the Cable News Network (CNN), the first 24-hour, all-news television network in 1980. AP The president also took aim at the current owners of the network, saying they had “destroyed Turner’s baby” and saying he hoped its next owners will be able to “bring it back to its former glory and credibility”. CNN is set to change hands again soon, with Trump supporter David Ellison’s Paramount Skydance reaching a deal to acquire CNN’s parent company Warner Bros earlier this year. CNN’s chief international anchor Christian Amanpour, who has been at the network since 1983, paid tribute to Turner.



“Remember when giants strode the world? Ted Turner was a giant,” she said. “He said it like it was and like it is, and we were his willing foot soldiers. And I think he changed not just the world, but all of our lives, too.” Turner’s signature achievement was creating the Cable News Network (CNN), the first 24-hour, all-news television network in 1980. View post on X In part, Turner’s own frustration with television news was the instigator. He often worked past 8pm, after the ABC, CBS and NBC nightly newscasts had already gone off the air.



He took a chance by starting the operation in the early days of cable television, living in an apartment above its Atlanta office. CNN’s breakthrough moment came during the Gulf War with Iraq in 1991. Most television journalists had fled Baghdad, but CNN stayed, capturing arresting images of a war’s outbreak. Turner was promised a continued role in CNN after his company’s sale to Time Warner but was gradually pushed out, much to his regret. “The mistake I made was losing control of the company,” he later said. Turner’s rise from uni dropout to media mogul



Robert Edward Turner III was born November 19, 1938, in Cincinnati. When he was nine, his family moved to Savannah, Georgia, where he grew up. After being expelled from Brown University, Turner came to Atlanta to work for his domineering father’s billboard company, Turner Advertising. After his father’s 1963 suicide, Turner took over the company. In 1970, he bought an independent UHF station with a weak signal that didn’t even cover Atlanta. Ted Turner is seen at his desk inside the CNN Centre in 1982. AP On December 17, 1976, he began transmitting the station to cable systems across the country via satellite. It became the TBS SuperStation. TBS’ motley collection of old movies and sitcom reruns was augmented by Turner’s acquisition of baseball’s Atlanta Braves. Perennial doormats, the Braves slowly attracted fans nationwide through their superstation exposure.



In the 1980s, Turner went deeply into debt to buy MGM, a move again greeted with scepticism. But the acquisition gave his company a library of vintage movies that eventually were parlayed into the TNT and Turner Classic Movies networks. ‘The mistake I made was losing control of the company.’ Ted Turner He revealed his ambitions as a younger man: “I used to tell people I wanted to become the world’s greatest sailor, businessman and lover all at the same time.” For much of his life a partying roustabout who wooed beautiful women, the lean, mustachioed sportsman married three times. He was married to Fonda from 1991 to 2001. She tired of his philandering and divorced him, although they remained friends. Perhaps Turner’s greatest love was for the land. He acquired millions of acres in ranches complete with roaming buffalo and was Nebraska’s largest private landholder. Researchers at Texas A&M University credited his donation of a few bulls in 2005 with helping increase the genetic diversity of the last herd of southern Plains bison.



Related Article Vale ‘It was beautiful’: In his last hours, James Valentine delivered one final performance He had a net worth of $US2.5 billion in 2023 but had dropped off Forbes magazine’s ranking of the 400 richest Americans in 2021. “See, my life is more an adventure than a quest to make money,” Turner once said. Turner managed to insult many with his shoot-from-the-lip style. An atheist since his only sister died of lupus at age 17, he called Christians “losers” and “Jesus freaks,” later apologising for both remarks. Turner grabbed a leadership role in American philanthropy with his 1997 pledge to give $US1 billion to UN charities. He joined former US Senator Sam Nunn to start the Nuclear Threat Initiative, a US-based nonprofit dedicated to reducing the threat of nuclear, biological and chemical weapons.



AP, Reuters The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: ASX set to jump as oil tumbles and sharemarkets rally on Iran deal hopes
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to jump as oil tumbles and sharemarkets rally on Iran deal hopes Stan Choe Updated May 7, 2026 — 6:44am ,first published 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oil prices sank, and stock markets rallied worldwide with hopes that the United States and Iran are nearing a deal to allow ships to deliver crude from the Persian Gulf once again to their customers. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, fell 7.8 per cent to $US101.27, down from more than $US115 early this week. It dropped as President Donald Trump said the Strait of Hormuz could be “OPEN TO ALL” if Iran accepts a reported agreement that the US president did not detail. Stocks around the world bounced higher and oil tumbled. AP The small strait has caused big trouble for the global economy because the war with Iran has blocked oil tankers from using it to exit the Persian Gulf. A reopening could allow oil to flow freely again and remove upward pressure on inflation that’s driving prices up for all kinds of products worldwide. On Wall Street, the S&P 500 climbed 1.5 per cent for its best day in nearly a month and hit another all-time high. The Dow Jones jumped 612 points, or 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 2 per cent to its own record. The Australian sharemarket is set to jump, with futures at 4.54am AEST pointing to a jump of 105 points, or 1.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX surged by 1.3 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar jumped and is trading at US72.40¢.



Related Article Dating Tinder boasts of astrology-led revival as singles events flourish Stock markets abroad had even bigger gains, with indexes leaping 6.5 per cent in Seoul, 2.9 per cent in Paris and 2.1 per cent in London. Of course, hopes have risen several times already on Wall Street about a possible end to the war with Iran, only to get dashed each time. That could happen again, and oil prices pared some of their steepest losses from Wednesday morning. The price for a barrel of Brent briefly dove below $97 before returning above $100 after Trump threatened to start bombing “at a much higher level and intensity” if Iran does not accept the agreement. Wall Street nevertheless latched onto some potentially encouraging signals. Trump said Tuesday he was pausing his effort to forcefully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial ships. And China’s foreign minister called for a comprehensive ceasefire following a meeting with Iran’s foreign minister. That could be influential because of how closely tied Iran is to China economically and politically.



In the meantime, big US companies continue to turn in much stronger profits for the start of 2026 than analysts expected. That’s supporting the stock market despite all the uncertainties created by the war. AMD helped lead the market with a surge of 18.6 per cent after it joined the list of big-name companies topping expectations for both profit and revenue. CEO Lisa Su said the chip company benefited from continued growth from artificial-intelligence technology, which is demanding tremendous amounts of computing power from data centers. AMD also said its revenue growth could accelerate in the current quarter to roughly 46 per cent from a year earlier. Another company enmeshed in the AI industry, Super Micro Computer, rallied 24.5 per cent after likewise delivering stronger earnings than analysts expected. Nvidia, the chip company that became the poster child of the AI boom, rose 5.7 per cent and was the single strongest force lifting the S&P 500 because of its immense size. CVS Health climbed 7.6 per cent after delivering better results for the first quarter than analysts expected and raising its financial forecasts for the full year. Disney gained 7.5 per cent after saying its “Zootopia 2” movie helped draw people to its streaming business, parks and cruise ships, while delivering a better-than-expected profit. Uber Technologies drove 8.5 per cent higher after giving a bookings forecast for the spring that was higher than analysts expected.



Outside of earnings reports, companies with big fuel bills jumped on hopes that oil prices will continue to ease. That included gains of 6.8 per cent for United Airlines, 6.8 per cent for Carnival and 8.8 per cent for Royal Caribbean. Related Article Opinion

AI Trump goes ‘woke’ with a sudden change of mind Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist All told, the S&P 500 rose 105.90 points to 7,365.12. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 612.34 to 49,910.59, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 512.82 to 25,838.94. In the bond market, Treasury yields sank as falling oil prices took pressure off inflation. The yield on the 10-year Treasury dropped to 4.35 per cent from 4.43 per cent late Tuesday. That’s a notable move for the bond market. Lower yields can bring down rates for mortgages and other kinds of loans going to US households and businesses, which in turn can give the economy a boost. Lower yields also tend to push upward on prices for stocks and other kinds of investments. The 10-year yield, though, remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from just before the war.



In stock markets abroad, South Korea’s Kospi jumped above the 7,000 level for the first time to a record thanks to big gains for AI winners, including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
